sections.title: The Zener Diode
sections.summary: Designed to operate in reverse breakdown with a stable V_Z. Below ~5 V → zener breakdown mechanism; above ~5 V → avalanche. Zener impedance Z_Z = ΔV_Z / ΔI_Z (requires a CHANGE in V and I — cannot be found from a single point).

sections.title: Zener Diode Applications
sections.summary: Voltage regulation: zener clamps V_OUT ≈ V_Z as long as it stays in breakdown. I_T = (V_IN − V_Z)/R splits between zener (I_Z) and load (I_L = V_Z/R_L). Also used as a limiter/clipper to clamp signal peaks.

sections.title: The Varactor Diode
sections.summary: Reverse-biased pn junction acting as a voltage-controlled capacitor. Increasing reverse voltage widens the depletion region → DECREASES capacitance (inverse relationship). Used in tuned LC circuits where f_r = 1/(2π√(LC)).

sections.title: Optical Diodes (LED, OLED, Photodiode)
sections.summary: LEDs emit light via electroluminescence under FORWARD bias; IR LEDs have longer wavelengths than visible LEDs. OLEDs use organic emissive layers and can be inkjet-printed. Photodiodes operate in REVERSE bias — reverse current rises with incident light intensity, internal resistance drops.

sections.title: The Solar Cell
sections.summary: Silicon PV cell produces ~0.5–0.6 V regardless of size. Series connection → more voltage (same current). Parallel connection → more current (same voltage). Solar arrays feed a charge controller or inverter, not the load directly.

sections.title: Other Types of Diodes
sections.summary: Laser diodes produce coherent, monochromatic, directional light. Tunnel diodes exhibit a negative-resistance region (used in oscillators). Schottky and hot-carrier diodes feature fast switching and low forward drop. Proper system operation requires correct biasing, connection, and interfacing.

questions.text: The zener diode normally operates in reverse breakdown.
questions.explanation: Zener diodes are specifically designed to operate in reverse breakdown, where V_Z stays nearly constant over a range of zener currents — that's what makes them useful as voltage regulators.

questions.text: A zener diode can be used as a voltage regulator.
questions.explanation: Voltage regulation is the primary application of zener diodes. The zener clamps V_OUT ≈ V_Z as long as it stays in breakdown.

questions.text: There is no current when a zener is in reverse breakdown.
questions.explanation: FALSE. There IS significant current — the zener current I_Z varies while V_Z stays approximately constant. That current flow is exactly what enables regulation.

questions.text: The varactor diode normally operates in forward bias.
questions.explanation: FALSE. The varactor operates in REVERSE bias, where the depletion region acts as the dielectric of the junction capacitance.

questions.text: The varactor diode is used as a variable capacitor.
questions.explanation: A varactor is a voltage-controlled variable capacitor — used in RF tuners, VCOs, and any circuit where capacitance needs to be adjusted electrically.

questions.text: The capacitance of a varactor varies directly with reverse voltage.
questions.explanation: FALSE — INVERSE relationship. As V_R increases, the depletion region widens, so capacitance DECREASES (C = εA/d, with d = depletion width). Common gotcha.

questions.text: The LED is based on the process of electroluminescence.
questions.explanation: Electroluminescence is the emission of photons when electrons recombine with holes across the LED's pn junction.

questions.text: The LED is normally operated in forward bias.
questions.explanation: Forward bias drives the electron-hole recombination that produces light. (Compare to photodiodes, which operate in reverse bias.)

questions.text: OLED stands for operational light-emitting diode.
questions.explanation: FALSE. OLED = ORGANIC Light-Emitting Diode. Uses organic compounds for the electroluminescent layer (instead of a traditional pn junction).

questions.text: The photodiode operates in reverse bias.
questions.explanation: Photodiodes operate in reverse bias. Incident light generates electron-hole pairs that increase the reverse current (λ-current).

questions.text: The reverse current of a photodiode increases as the incident light increases.
questions.explanation: More photons → more electron-hole pairs generated → larger reverse current. This linear photoresponse is what makes photodiodes useful as light detectors.

questions.text: The light emitted by a laser diode is monochromatic.
questions.explanation: Laser light has three defining properties: monochromatic (single wavelength), coherent (in-phase), and highly directional.

questions.text: A solar cell typically produces about 0.5 V.
questions.explanation: A typical silicon PV cell produces ~0.5–0.6 V regardless of cell area. (Area affects current output, not voltage.)

questions.text: PV cells connected in series produce more current than a single cell.
questions.explanation: FALSE. Series connection increases VOLTAGE, not current. Current through series cells equals the current of a single cell. (For more current, connect in parallel.)

questions.text: PV cells connected in parallel produce less voltage than a single cell.
questions.explanation: FALSE. Parallel connection produces the SAME voltage as a single cell — it does not reduce voltage. Parallel increases CURRENT.

questions.explanation: Figure 3-11 is the basic zener regulator. Ideally V_OUT = V_Z regardless of V_IN (as long as it stays in breakdown). That's the point of regulation.

questions.text: If the input voltage in Figure 3–14 is reduced by 2 V, the zener current will
questions.explanation: I_T = (V_IN − V_Z)/R drops with V_IN. Since I_L = V_Z/R_L is fixed (V_Z regulated), I_Z = I_T − I_L must DECREASE.

questions.text: If R_L in Figure 3–14 is removed, the current through the zener diode will
questions.explanation: With R_L removed (open), I_L = 0, so all source current flows through the zener: I_Z = I_T. The zener now carries the full current that was previously split with the load.

questions.text: If the zener opens in Figure 3–14, the output voltage will
questions.explanation: With the zener open, the regulator becomes a simple voltage divider: V_OUT = V_IN · R_L/(R + R_L). Since V_IN must be greater than V_Z for regulation, V_OUT rises above the previously regulated V_Z level.

questions.text: If R in Figure 3–14 is increased, the current to the load resistor will
questions.explanation: Classic gotcha. As long as the zener stays in regulation, V_OUT = V_Z is constant, so I_L = V_Z/R_L is unaffected by R. (R only affects how much current is 'left over' for the zener.)

questions.text: If the input voltage amplitude in Figure 3–18(a) is increased, the positive output voltage will
questions.explanation: Figure 3-18(a) is a zener limiter clamping the positive peaks at V_Z + 0.7 V. Increasing input amplitude doesn't raise the clipped output level — that's what a limiter does.

questions.text: If the input voltage amplitude in Figure 3–19(a) is reduced, the amplitude of the output voltage will
questions.explanation: Figure 3-19(a) is a back-to-back zener limiter. Reducing input amplitude below the clipping threshold means output simply follows the reduced input → output amplitude DECREASES.

questions.text: If the varactor capacitance is increased in Figure 3–26, the resonant frequency will
questions.explanation: f_r = 1/(2π√(LC)). C increases → f_r DECREASES (inverse-square-root relationship).

questions.text: If the reverse voltage across the varactor in Figure 3–26 is increased, the frequency will
questions.explanation: Two-step reasoning: V_R↑ → depletion widens → C DECREASES → f_r = 1/(2π√(LC)) INCREASES. Common test question — chains two inverse relationships.

questions.text: If the bias voltage in Figure 3–30 is increased, the light output of the LED will
questions.explanation: More forward bias → more forward current → more electron-hole recombinations → more photons → brighter output. (Linear-ish until current limits are exceeded.)

questions.text: If the bias voltage in Figure 3–30 is reversed, the light output of the LED will
questions.explanation: Reversing bias puts the LED in reverse bias, which blocks forward current. No recombination → no light. Light output drops to ~zero, which counts as a decrease.

questions.text: A certain solar cell produces 0.5 V. If the light intensity decreases, the current to a fixed load will
questions.explanation: Less light → fewer electron-hole pairs generated in the PV cell → less photocurrent delivered to the fixed load.

questions.text: The cathode of a zener diode in a voltage regulator is normally
questions.explanation: A zener regulator operates in reverse bias, so the cathode (n-side) is at higher potential than the anode (p-side).

questions.text: If a certain zener diode has a zener voltage of 3.6 V, it operates in
questions.explanation: V_Z = 3.6 V is below the ~5 V threshold. Below 5 V → zener breakdown mechanism dominates; above 5 V → avalanche breakdown dominates. Key principle for the midterm.

questions.text: For a certain 12 V zener diode, a 10 mA change in zener current produces a 0.1 V change in zener voltage. The zener impedance for this current range is
questions.explanation: Z_Z = ΔV_Z / ΔI_Z = 0.1 V / 10 mA = 10 Ω. (Note: textbook prints these options with units of 'V' — that's a typo; the correct unit is ohms.)

questions.text: The datasheet for a particular zener gives V_Z = 10 V at I_Z = 500 mA. Z_Z for these conditions is
questions.explanation: Z_Z requires a CHANGE in voltage and current (ΔV/ΔI). A single operating point alone cannot determine zener impedance. Key principle.

questions.text: A no-load condition means that
questions.explanation: No-load means the output terminals are open, which is equivalent to R_L = ∞ (infinite resistance). Both descriptions are correct.

questions.text: A varactor diode exhibits
options: a variable capacitance that depends on reverse voltage
a variable resistance that depends on reverse voltage
a variable capacitance that depends on forward current
a constant capacitance over a range of reverse voltages
questions.explanation: Definition of a varactor: voltage-controlled capacitance via depletion-region width modulation under REVERSE bias.

questions.text: An LED
questions.explanation: LEDs emit light via electroluminescence during forward-bias recombination. (Option (b) describes a photodiode, not an LED.)

questions.text: Compared to a visible red LED, an infrared LED
options: produces only one color of light
questions.explanation: Infrared (>700 nm) has LONGER wavelengths than visible red (~620–700 nm). Longer wavelength = lower frequency = lower energy photons.

questions.text: Compared to incandescent bulbs, high-intensity LEDs
questions.explanation: High-intensity LEDs are brighter, last much longer (~50,000+ hours vs. ~1,000 for incandescent), and use less power. (Note: textbook prints option labels with two '(c)'s — a typo. Correct answer is 'all of the above'.)

questions.text: An OLED differs from a conventional LED in that it
options: has layers of organic material in the place of a pn junction
can be implemented using an inkjet printing process
questions.explanation: OLEDs use organic emissive layers instead of a traditional pn junction AND can be deposited via inkjet printing — a key manufacturing advantage. They still require bias voltage, so (a) is wrong.

questions.text: An infrared LED is optically coupled to a photodiode. When the LED is turned off, the reading on an ammeter in series with the reverse-biased photodiode will
questions.explanation: LED off → no incident IR light on the photodiode → no photogenerated electron-hole pairs → reverse current drops back to dark current (small leakage). (Note: textbook prints option labels with two '(c)'s — a typo. Correct answer is 'decrease'.)

questions.text: The internal resistance of a photodiode
options: increases with light intensity when reverse-biased
decreases with light intensity when reverse-biased
increases with light intensity when forward-biased
decreases with light intensity when forward-biased
questions.explanation: More light → more carriers generated → photodiode becomes more conductive → internal resistance DROPS. This is the basis for using photodiodes as light-controlled current sources in REVERSE bias.

questions.text: The bottom layer of a solar cell is
questions.explanation: The bottom layer is the back contact / conductive layer that collects current. The pn junction sits above it, with the n region typically at the top (light-facing) side.

questions.text: The usable voltage from a silicon solar cell is approximately
questions.explanation: Silicon PV cells produce ~0.5–0.6 V regardless of size. (Matches the T/F principle that solar cell voltage is ~0.5 V.)

questions.text: In a solar array, the load is usually a
questions.explanation: Solar arrays feed a charge controller (for battery systems) or an inverter (for grid/AC loads), not the final load directly.

questions.text: A laser diode produces
questions.explanation: Laser light is COHERENT (in-phase) AND MONOCHROMATIC (single wavelength). Both are defining properties — along with being highly directional.

questions.text: A diode that has a negative resistance characteristic is the
questions.explanation: Tunnel diodes exhibit a negative-resistance region (current decreases as voltage increases over a range) due to quantum tunneling. Used in high-frequency oscillators.

questions.text: In order for a system to function properly, the various types of circuits that make up the system must be
questions.explanation: A working system requires correct biasing (DC operating points), correct connections (signal paths), AND correct interfacing (impedance matching, level shifting, etc.). All three are necessary.
